items.explanation: Rolling friction is the resistance to motion that acts when one body rolls over the surface of another. It is always less than sliding friction because a rolling object makes only brief point contact with the surface rather than continuous surface contact. Static friction acts on stationary objects; sliding friction acts on sliding objects; fluid friction (drag) acts on objects moving through fluids.

options.A: Rolling > Sliding > Static

items.explanation: Static friction is the largest because it must fully overcome the interlocking of irregularities when an object is at rest. Sliding friction is slightly less — once sliding begins, contact points don't have time to fully interlock. Rolling friction is the smallest — a rolling body makes only brief point contact, so very little interlocking occurs. Correct order (largest to smallest): Static > Sliding > Rolling.

items.question: Heavy machinery is moved by placing logs under it. This works because:

items.question: Rolling friction compared to sliding friction is:

options.A: Equal in magnitude for the same object
options.B: Greater because rolling involves more surface area
options.C: Smaller because a rolling body makes only brief point contact

items.explanation: Rolling friction is always smaller than sliding friction. A rolling body makes contact with the surface only at a single point (or very small area) at any instant, and this contact point changes continuously. So the irregularities have very little time to interlock. In contrast, a sliding body has continuous surface contact with extensive interlocking. Therefore, rolling friction is much less than sliding friction. This is the scientific basis for wheels, ball bearings, and rollers.

items.question: In which of the following machine components are ball bearings most commonly used?

options.A: Electric wires that carry current to motors
options.B: Between hub and axle in ceiling fans and bicycle wheels

At these points, there is relative rotational motion between two parts. Without ball bearings, this would create large sliding friction. Ball bearings convert this to rolling friction, reducing energy waste and wear. Electric wires, light bulbs, and batteries do not involve surface-to-surface friction of this type.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The frictional force exerted by fluids (liquids and gases) on objects moving through them is called fluid friction. This is also called DRAG.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Fluids include both liquids (water) and gases (air).
Air is very light and thin, yet it exerts frictional force on objects moving through it.
Similarly, water and other liquids exert friction on objects moving through them.
The frictional force on an object in a fluid depends on:
(i) The speed of the object with respect to the fluid (faster = more drag).
(ii) The shape of the object (streamlined shapes experience less drag).
(iii) The nature of the fluid (denser/thicker fluids exert more drag).
To minimize fluid friction, objects moving through fluids are given special streamlined shapes.
Birds and fishes have naturally evolved streamlined body shapes to reduce fluid friction and conserve energy.
Vehicles (aeroplanes, cars, ships, submarines) are designed to have streamlined shapes to minimize drag and improve fuel efficiency (Fig. 9.17 — similarity between aeroplane shape and bird shape).
"Fluids exert force of friction on objects in motion through them."
The frictional force exerted by fluids is also called drag.

items.question: What is fluid friction? What is it also called?
items.answer:
Fluid friction is the frictional force exerted by fluids (liquids and gases) on objects moving through them.
It is also called DRAG.
Fluids include both liquids (such as water) and gases (such as air). When an object moves through a fluid, the fluid exerts a resistance force (fluid friction/drag) opposing the motion of the object.

items.question: On what factors does the frictional force on an object in a fluid depend?
items.answer:
The frictional force (drag) on an object moving in a fluid depends on:
1. Speed of the object: The faster the object moves through the fluid, the greater is the drag acting on it.
2. Shape of the object: Streamlined (smooth, tapered) shapes experience less drag than blunt or irregular shapes.
3. Nature of the fluid: Denser or thicker fluids (like water) exert more drag than lighter fluids (like air).

items.question: Why are objects moving through fluids given special streamlined shapes? Give two examples.
items.answer:
Objects moving through fluids are given streamlined (special) shapes to minimize fluid friction (drag).
When an object has a streamlined shape, it can cut through the fluid smoothly. The fluid flows around the object without creating large resistance. Less energy is lost in overcoming fluid friction.
If blunt or irregular shapes are used, the fluid cannot flow smoothly, creating large drag and more energy loss.

EXAMPLES:
1. Aeroplanes: The body of an aeroplane is long, tapered, and smooth. It is designed to minimize air resistance (drag) so the plane can fly efficiently (Fig. 9.17).
2. Fish: The body of a fish is naturally streamlined (tapered at both ends). This shape allows fish to move through water with minimal resistance, conserving their energy.
(Additional: birds, submarines, and fast cars also have streamlined shapes.)

items.question: Why do birds and fish have streamlined body shapes? How does this relate to fluid friction?
items.answer:
Birds and fish move through fluids (air and water respectively) all the time. Their bodies have evolved naturally to have streamlined shapes.

FISH:
Fish need to move through water, which is dense and exerts strong drag.
A fish's body is tapered at both ends (streamlined). This shape allows water to flow smoothly around the body with minimal turbulence.
Result: Fish face less fluid friction (drag) and can swim efficiently without wasting too much energy.

BIRDS:
Birds fly through air. A bird's body is tapered from head to tail (streamlined).
This shape allows air to flow smoothly around the bird's body with minimal air resistance.
Result: Birds face less drag and can fly efficiently over long distances.

RELATION TO FLUID FRICTION:
Streamlined shapes reduce fluid friction because they allow the fluid to flow around the object smoothly. Objects that are not streamlined (blunt shapes) cause turbulence in the fluid, greatly increasing drag and energy consumption.

items.question: What is drag? Explain how it affects vehicles and how it is minimized.
items.answer:
DRAG:
Drag is the frictional force exerted by fluids (liquids and gases) on objects moving through them. It is also called fluid friction.
Drag acts in the direction opposite to the direction of motion of the object.
Drag depends on the speed, shape of the object, and nature of the fluid.

HOW DRAG AFFECTS VEHICLES:
All vehicles moving through air (aeroplanes, cars, trains) experience drag.
Drag acts opposite to the direction of motion, resisting the vehicle's movement.
At higher speeds, drag is much greater, requiring more fuel/energy to maintain speed.
Drag wastes energy (fuel) and slows vehicles down.
Ships and submarines moving through water face even greater drag due to the density of water.

HOW DRAG IS MINIMIZED:
Streamlined shapes: Vehicles are designed with smooth, tapered shapes to minimize turbulence and allow fluid to flow smoothly around them.
- Aeroplanes: Long, tapered fuselage reduces air drag.
- Fast cars: Low, tapered bodies reduce air resistance.
- Submarines: Rounded, elongated shape reduces water drag.
- Bullets and rockets: Pointed, tapered shapes to cut through air with minimal drag.
By minimizing drag, fuel efficiency improves and higher speeds are achievable.

items.question: Compare fluid friction with other types of friction. In which situations does fluid friction become significant?
items.answer:
COMPARISON:
Static friction: Acts when object at rest, trying to move. Largest of contact frictions.
Sliding friction: Acts when object slides on surface. Less than static.
Rolling friction: Acts when object rolls on surface. Less than sliding.
Fluid friction (drag): Acts when object moves through a fluid. Depends on speed and shape.

DIFFERENCES:
- Contact friction (static, sliding, rolling): Acts between solid surfaces.
- Fluid friction (drag): Acts between a solid object and a fluid (liquid or gas).
- Fluid friction increases with speed (faster motion = more drag), while contact friction is generally independent of speed.
- Fluid friction depends on the shape of the object (streamlined shapes = less drag).

WHEN FLUID FRICTION IS SIGNIFICANT:
1. High-speed vehicles: At high speeds (aeroplanes, race cars), air drag becomes the dominant force to overcome.
2. Underwater motion: Fish, submarines, and ships moving through water face significant water drag (water is ~800 times denser than air).
3. Falling objects: A parachute uses air drag to slow a person's fall to a safe speed.
4. Sports: Cyclists, swimmers, and runners experience significant fluid friction at high speeds.
5. Fluids of high density: Moving through oil, honey, or other thick fluids involves even greater drag.

items.question: Explain in detail how streamlined shapes help birds, fish, and vehicles reduce fluid friction. What would happen if vehicles had non-streamlined shapes?
items.answer:
FLUID FRICTION AND STREAMLINED SHAPES:
When an object moves through a fluid, the fluid exerts a frictional force (drag) opposing the motion. The amount of drag depends on the shape of the object.
- Streamlined shapes: The fluid flows smoothly around the object with minimal turbulence. Less drag is created.
- Non-streamlined (blunt) shapes: The fluid cannot flow smoothly. It separates from the surface and creates turbulence (swirling currents). This creates much more drag.

HOW BIRDS ARE STREAMLINED:
A bird's body is tapered from head to tail. The head is rounded at the front and the body narrows toward the tail.
Air flows smoothly over the bird's body as it flies.
Minimal turbulence is created behind the bird.
Result: Low air resistance, efficient flight, less energy spent.

HOW FISH ARE STREAMLINED:
A fish's body is tapered at both ends (front and rear).
Water flows smoothly around the fish as it swims.
Very little turbulence is created around the fish's body.
Result: Low water resistance, smooth swimming with little energy waste.

HOW VEHICLES ARE STREAMLINED:
AEROPLANES (Fig. 9.17): Their long, tapered fuselage and swept-back wings allow air to flow over and around them smoothly. This minimizes air drag at high speeds and allows efficient flight.
FAST CARS (racing cars): Low, wedge-shaped body. Air flows over the top smoothly. Less turbulence means less drag.
SUBMARINES: Rounded, elongated shape tapers at both ends. Water flows smoothly around the hull. Less water drag means less fuel needed for underwater travel.
BULLETS AND ROCKETS: Pointed nose allows them to cut through air with minimal drag.

IF VEHICLES HAD NON-STREAMLINED SHAPES:
- Very large drag would be created.
- Vehicles would need enormous amounts of energy (fuel) to overcome this drag.
- Maximum speed would be severely limited.
- Fuel efficiency would be very poor.
- Aeroplanes would not be able to fly (drag would exceed lift at any practical speed).
- Submarines would be very slow and inefficient.

---

items.explanation: Fish have naturally evolved streamlined (tapered at both ends) body shapes to reduce fluid friction (drag) while swimming through water. items.question: In science, the common name for both gases and liquids is:

items.explanation: In science, fluids is the common term for both liquids and gases. Both can flow and exert friction on objects moving through them. Solids have a fixed shape and do not flow. Vapours specifically refers to a gas-phase substance near its condensation point. Mixtures can be solid, liquid, or gas combinations. When we talk about fluid friction (drag), we mean the friction exerted by any liquid or gas.

items.question: Fluid friction (drag) depends on:

items.explanation: Fluid friction (drag) depends on three factors: (1) Speed of the object — faster objects experience more drag; (2) Shape of the object — streamlined shapes experience less drag than blunt shapes; (3) Nature of the fluid — denser/thicker fluids (like water) exert more drag than lighter fluids (like air). Colour and weight are not direct factors in determining drag.

items.question: As an object moves faster through a fluid, the drag on it:

options.A: Decreases because faster objects cut through fluid more easily
options.B: Stays the same regardless of speed
options.C: Increases because faster motion encounters more fluid resistance
options.D: Becomes zero at very high speeds

items.explanation: Drag increases with the speed of the object. The faster an object moves through a fluid, the more fluid molecules it encounters per second, and the more resistance (drag) it faces. This is why aeroplanes consume much more fuel at higher speeds — they must overcome greater air drag. Drag definitely does not decrease or become zero at high speed; it increases significantly.

items.question: Which shape experiences LESS fluid friction (drag)?

options.A: Blunt/flat front surface facing the fluid
options.B: Irregular, angular shape
options.C: Streamlined (tapered, smooth) shape

items.explanation: A streamlined (tapered) shape allows fluid to flow smoothly around the object with minimal turbulence. Less turbulence means less drag. Blunt, irregular, or cube-shaped objects cause the fluid to separate from the surface and create swirling turbulence (eddies) behind the object, greatly increasing drag. This is why aeroplanes, fish, birds, submarines, and fast cars all have streamlined shapes.

items.question: Why are vehicles (aeroplanes, submarines, fast cars) specifically designed with streamlined shapes?

(d) wet marble floor, dry marble floor, towel, newspaper.

EXERCISE ANSWER: (a) wet marble floor, dry marble floor, newspaper and towel.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: Wet marble floor is the smoothest surface (water reduces friction), so friction is least. Dry marble floor is smooth but has slightly more friction than wet marble. Newspaper is rougher than marble floor. Towel is the roughest of the four, so friction is greatest on it. Increasing order: Wet marble < Dry marble < Newspaper < Towel.

---

EXERCISE 4: Suppose your writing desk is tilted a little. A book kept on it starts sliding down. Show the direction of frictional force acting on it.

EXERCISE ANSWER: When the book slides DOWN the inclined (tilted) desk, the force of friction acts UP the inclined surface (opposing the direction of motion).
The book slides downward due to gravity. Friction always opposes the direction of motion. So friction acts upward along the surface of the desk, opposing the downward sliding of the book.

---

EXERCISE 5: You spill a bucket of soapy water on a marble floor accidently. Would it make it easier or more difficult for you to walk on the floor? Why?

EXERCISE ANSWER: It would make it MORE DIFFICULT (and dangerous) to walk on the floor.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: Soapy water acts as a lubricant on the smooth marble floor. It forms a thin, slippery layer between the soles of your shoes and the marble surface. This greatly reduces the friction between your foot and the floor. Without sufficient friction, your feet cannot grip the floor. You would slip and fall easily. Friction is necessary for walking; reducing it makes walking difficult and unsafe.

---

EXERCISE 6: Explain why sportsmen use shoes with spikes.

EXERCISE ANSWER: Sportsmen use shoes with spikes to INCREASE friction between their shoes and the ground.
During intense sports activities (running, jumping, playing football, athletics), sportsmen need to run fast, change direction quickly, and push off the ground hard. If friction is low, their shoes would slip on the ground, making it impossible to run or change direction effectively.
The spikes are sharp projections on the sole. They dig into the soft ground (grass, track), dramatically increasing the friction force. With spikes, athletes get a firm grip on the ground, helping them run faster, change direction easily, and perform better. This is an example of deliberately increasing friction.

---

EXERCISE 7: Iqbal has to push a lighter box and Seema has to push a similar heavier box on the same floor. Who will have to apply a larger force and why?

EXERCISE ANSWER: SEEMA will have to apply a larger force to push the heavier box.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: Friction depends on how hard the two surfaces are pressed together. A heavier box presses down on the floor with a greater force (due to greater weight/gravity). This causes the irregularities on the box's surface to press more firmly against the irregularities on the floor, resulting in stronger interlocking. This means greater friction acts on the heavier box. To overcome this greater friction, Seema needs to apply a larger force. Iqbal's lighter box exerts less pressing force on the floor, resulting in less friction, so he needs less force to push it.

---

EXERCISE 8: Explain why sliding friction is less than static friction.

EXERCISE ANSWER: Sliding friction is less than static friction because of the following reason:
When a box is at rest on the floor, the irregularities on the surface of the box have sufficient time to interlock deeply and firmly with the irregularities on the floor surface. To break this interlocking and start the box moving requires overcoming static friction, which is the maximum friction.
Once the box starts sliding, the contact points on the surface of the box do not get enough time to interlock with the contact points on the floor (they pass over each other too quickly). The interlocking is less firm during sliding than when the box was at rest.
Therefore, less force is needed to keep the box sliding than to start it moving.
Result: Sliding friction is slightly smaller than static friction.

---

EXERCISE 9: Give examples to show that friction is both a friend and a foe.

EXERCISE ANSWER:
FRICTION AS A FRIEND (useful examples):
1. Walking: Friction between the soles of our shoes and the floor allows us to walk without slipping. On a wet, slippery floor, reduced friction makes walking difficult.
2. Writing: Friction between chalk and the blackboard allows chalk particles to rub off and stick to the board, enabling writing. Friction between pen nib and paper allows writing on paper.
3. Holding objects: We can hold a glass, pen, or kulhar because friction between our fingers and the object prevents it from slipping.
4. Nails and knots: Nails are fixed in walls due to friction. Knots in rope are held by friction.
5. Brakes: Friction between brake pads and wheel rims allows vehicles to slow down and stop safely.

FRICTION AS A FOE (harmful examples):
1. Wear and tear: Friction wears out the soles of shoes, screws, ball bearings, and machine parts. The steps of foot over-bridges at railway stations wear out due to friction from thousands of feet.
2. Heat and energy loss: Friction between moving machine parts generates heat, wasting energy. A mixer jar becomes hot because of friction between moving parts.
3. Matchstick fire: While this can be a useful example too, uncontrolled friction can cause fires (not always desired).

---

EXERCISE 10: Explain why objects moving in fluids must have special shapes.

EXERCISE ANSWER: Objects moving through fluids (liquids and gases) must have special streamlined shapes to minimize fluid friction (drag).
REASON:
When an object moves through a fluid, the fluid exerts a frictional force (drag) opposing its motion. The magnitude of this drag depends on the shape of the object.
- Non-streamlined (blunt) shapes: The fluid cannot flow smoothly around the object. It separates from the surface and creates turbulence (swirling currents). This greatly increases drag, requiring much more energy to maintain motion and limiting speed.
- Streamlined shapes: The fluid flows smoothly around the object with minimal turbulence. Drag is greatly reduced. Less energy is needed to maintain motion and higher speeds can be achieved.

EXAMPLES:
1. Fish: Fish have naturally streamlined bodies (tapered at both ends). This allows them to swim through water with minimal drag, saving energy.
2. Birds: Birds have tapered (streamlined) bodies. This reduces air resistance during flight.
3. Aeroplanes: Aeroplanes are designed with long, tapered, smooth fuselages (Fig. 9.17). The shape resembles a bird. This minimizes air drag and allows efficient high-speed flight with less fuel.
4. Submarines and ships: These have streamlined hulls to reduce water drag.
5. Bullets and rockets: Pointed, tapered shapes minimize air drag for higher speed.

CONCLUSION: Streamlined shapes are essential for efficient movement through fluids. Without them, vehicles would waste enormous amounts of energy, move slowly, and be impractical for use.

sections.text:
- BALL BEARING: Small metal balls placed between hub and axle to reduce friction by replacing sliding with rolling.
- DRAG: Frictional force exerted by fluids on objects moving through them; also called fluid friction.
- FLUID FRICTION: Friction exerted by fluids (liquids and gases) on moving objects; same as drag.
- FRICTION: Force that opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
- INTERLOCKING: The locking of irregularities on two surfaces into one another, which is the cause of friction.
- LUBRICANTS: Substances (oil, grease, graphite) applied between moving surfaces to reduce friction.
- ROLLING FRICTION: Friction when one body rolls over the surface of another; less than sliding friction.
- SLIDING FRICTION: Friction when one surface slides over another; less than static friction but more than rolling.
- STATIC FRICTION: Friction that acts when we try to move an object at rest; the largest type of contact friction.
